remarks: Are you buying grain, or have you come to tell me how to sell it?
The fish seller swears his fish are fresh. I recognise one of them from last Tuesday.
Watch the fish seller’s thumb on the scales. He presses it down, then charges you for the extra weight.
The fish next door have been there so long, I am beginning to feel obliged to feed them.
The finest minds in both churches have argued about reunion for years. My mother is of an opinion that they will not resolve this issue without consulting her.
My mother supports the Union. My brother supports the Union. My father does not. Sunday dinner now requires two tables.
Greek or Latin, everyone expects the baker to rise before dawn.
I asked the priest whether cheating with the scales was a sin. He said yes. Then he asked which merchant I meant, because he had bought fish that morning.
My wife takes a very long time whenever she visits the tanner. How many questions can a woman have about leather?
The tanner gave my wife a fine leather purse. Very generous. I should be happier if she had told me about it herself.
My wife says I hear only what suits me. An excellent woman. Always praising my judgement.
The Emperor should visit the market more often. Let him carry a sack of flour before he orders us to sell it for half the price.
If you see the Emperor, tell him the tax collector has already been. Twice. He seems to have forgotten the first visit.
You have the look of someone accustomed to giving orders. Try giving one for a sack of barley.
That is a fine cloak. Keep it covered when you bargain, or every merchant here will suddenly remember how poor he is.
No, the imperial eagle above my stall does not mean the palace pays my rent.
The price is written there. You can read it. I can see you deciding whether to admit that.
Credit? Certainly. Bring someone richer than yourself to guarantee it.
I know three men who claim to have spoken with the Sultan. They owe me money between them.
The Genoese buy by the shipload. The Venetians bargain over every handful. When payment is due, I have to chase both.
The merchant across the square says grain will be cheaper tomorrow. He would like you to wait until I go out of business.
Mind the cat. She works here. The boy is merely related to me.
Take the beans. Your household will eat well, though your neighbours may regret it.
That loaf is for the widow by the fountain. Choose another; I have put it aside.
That old soldier insists on paying me when his wages arrive. I have stopped asking which emperor owes them.
People tell me everything at this stall. Then they ask whether I know any news.
You keep looking at me as though I ought to say something memorable. Buy something. I shall remember that.
Go on, take a pinch and judge for yourself. I can endure an honest customer.
My youngest wants to become a philosopher. He can begin by explaining where yesterday’s takings went.
Last night I dreamed I was rich. Even in the dream, my landlord raised the rent.
A man offered me a sword for three sacks of grain. I asked whether the sword could feed my children.
I lent my cousin a cart. He returned one wheel and a very long story.
My son has learned to write. The first thing he wrote was a list of things he wants.
The rain comes through my roof. My landlord says I should be grateful for the fresh air.
I bought a better lock for the storeroom. My wife has put the key somewhere safe. We are both looking for it.
The guild sent a man to inspect my weights. He left with a free sack of barley. Apparently everything was in order.
A pickpocket tried to rob me yesterday. He looked in my purse and changed his mind.
Two Varangians bought breakfast here. By the time they left, I had sold enough to close for the day.
A cavalryman complained about the price of oats. He had no complaints about the price of wine. His horse looked disappointed.
A young archer told me he could hit a coin at fifty paces. I asked him to put one on the counter first.
That new recruit used to carry sacks for me. Now he carries a shield and tells me I must address him properly.
Every time they fire a cannon, the weights jump off my scales. If this continues, I shall send the gunners a bill.
A galley’s worth of rowers came looking for bread. Next time I shall ask the captain to warn the bakers before he enters the harbour.
The Genoese sailors asked whether I would take payment in foreign coin. I said yes. Then they asked whether I had any change in gold.
A Venetian galley arrived this morning. Before the ropes were tied, three men were arguing about what the harbour owed them.
A ship has brought three sorts of silk and no flour. Fine. We shall all look magnificent while we wait for the next one.
The cistern keeper says the water will last. I wish he would say it without looking up at the clouds.
The bathhouse has raised its prices again. A man must now choose whether to come home clean or eat supper.
I went into Hagia Sophia to pray for patience. A man stepped in front of me. The Lord wastes no time.
That chain across the harbour is a fine piece of work. Could we borrow a length for the tax collector’s door?
Galata looks so close from here. Try collecting a debt there. You will discover how wide the water is.
Our ancestors had room to race chariots in this city. I cannot get a cart past the cabbage stalls.
There is enough marble lying about Constantinople to build another palace. Somehow, my doorstep is still mud.
With all these church bells, nobody can claim to have overslept. My apprentice continues to try.
The palace has ordered more candles. Perhaps this time they will have enough light to find the money they owe me.
If arguing about God earns a place in heaven, the men outside the church have reserved the best seats.
My father says miracles still happen. He says he once paid a tax and was not asked for another.
My wife lights a candle before every difficult purchase. I would prefer her to ask the price first.

“A false balance is abomination to the Lord.” — Proverbs 11:1
The priest read that one while looking straight at the fish seller.

“Money answereth all things.” — Ecclesiastes 10:19
Then why will my wife never give me a straight answer about where it went?

“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” — Matthew 6:21
Mine is in the till. My wife says she has suspected that for years.
